transcript.content: Hello. What brings you into the clinic today?

Well, I came in because... it's just, it's been getting really bad lately. My mind, it just keeps going blank, completely blank, and always at the absolute worst times. I've been a crossing guard and flagger for a long time, you know? I have my bachelor's degree, but this job, it gets me outside, and I know exactly what I'm doing. Or, well, I used to. Lately, I'll be standing there, and I'll look down at the road-closure forms, the ones I've filled out a thousand times before, or I'll be holding the stop-slow paddle, and suddenly... nothing. It's like someone just wiped the slate clean. I cannot remember the steps. The steps I have done for years! I just stand there, staring at the paddle, and my brain is just empty. It's terrifying, honestly, because people are relying on me to keep them safe, to direct the traffic, and I'm just frozen, trying to force my brain to remember what 'slow' means or what I'm supposed to do next. I just don't understand why it's happening, but it's happening a lot.
When your mind goes blank like that, about how long does each episode usually last?

Oh, gosh, time is... it's really hard to say, honestly. Because when you're standing out there in the middle of a busy intersection, or right at the edge of a construction zone, and you have, you know, a huge line of F-150s and heavy dump trucks just idling there, waiting for you to flip the sign or wave them through... a few seconds can feel like an absolute eternity. I really don't have a stopwatch on me, obviously, and my phone is always tucked away in my high-vis vest pocket because we absolutely aren't allowed to have them out on the site—strict safety regulations and all that, which I totally respect. 

So I can't just check the time when it happens. I just... I stand there, and my heart starts pounding so hard in my ears, and I'm staring down at the asphalt, and I just don't know. Is it a minute? Is it five minutes? Is it just thirty seconds? I really couldn't give you a number. The foreman hasn't come over and yelled at me about holding up the line yet, so maybe it's shorter than it feels to me, but in my head... in my head, I'm just trapped in this endless, terrifying void where I can't even remember what the word 'stop' means, let alone keep track of how long I've been standing there. It's just so frustrating because I try to piece it together later when I get home, like, okay, the sun was hitting the pavement here, the cars were lined up there, but the blankness just completely swallows the whole concept of time for me. So, yeah, I really have no idea.
Outside of these specific freezing moments at work, have you noticed any other problems with your memory or day-to-day thinking?

Well, honestly, it's... it really is mostly just that exact thing I was talking about. Like, I don't feel like I'm losing my keys or forgetting people's names or anything like that. It's really just... it's just this terrifying thing where my mind just keeps going blank, completely blank, and like I said, always at the absolute worst times. It's just so specific to that. 

I'll be there, and I'll look at the road-closure forms—the ones we have to fill out for the county, you know, with the specific permit numbers and the traffic flow diagrams that I used to be able to sketch out in my sleep—or I'll be holding the stop-slow paddle, shifting its weight in my hands, and suddenly I just cannot remember the steps. The steps I have done for years! It's not like I'm forgetting what I had for breakfast, it's like the fundamental knowledge of how to do my job, how to process the information right in front of me, just evaporates. It's just... gone. The thinking part of my brain just shuts down completely in those moments. It's less about forgetting day-to-day things and more about this... this complete inability to think or process what I'm looking at when I need to the most.

Well, I mean, people are always watching me out there, right? That's kind of the whole point of the job. You're standing out in the middle of the road in a bright neon yellow and orange vest, the ones with the silver reflective tape all over the chest and arms, holding an oversized stop sign, so it's practically impossible for them not to look at you. The drivers, I mean. They stare at you because they're annoyed they have to stop, or they're trying to figure out how long the delay is going to be. You get guys in those big lifted trucks just glaring, tapping their steering wheels, and commuters peering over their dashboards looking stressed, and even the guys on the construction crew—the paving guys or the trench diggers—they're constantly glancing over to see if I'm holding the traffic properly so they don't get run over. 

So, I'm always being watched. Every single minute of my shift, eyes are on me. But... no, I really wouldn't say the episodes happen because they're watching me, or that I feel particularly scrutinized or judged right before my mind goes blank. It's not like I get nervous about them looking at me. I've been doing this for years, I have a bachelor's degree, I know how to handle myself, and I'm totally used to the stares, the angry looks, the impatient sighs out of rolled-down windows, all of it. 

The blankness... it just comes from somewhere else entirely. It's not like a stage fright thing at all. It's just, I'll be looking at the paddle, or looking down at those road-closure forms on my clipboard, the ones with the permit numbers, and it absolutely does not matter if there's one single car on a quiet backroad or fifty cars backed up at a major intersection staring right at me... the slate just wipes itself clean anyway. The steps just evaporate. I don't feel them watching me and then freeze up. It's just this awful, terrifying empty void that happens inside my own head, and it completely disconnects me from everything, regardless of who happens to be sitting in their car looking at me at the time. So, no, I really don't think it has anything to do with people watching.
Outside of work, do you find yourself constantly worrying about a variety of everyday things, like family, finances, or health, more days than not?

No, not really. I mean, I have the normal stuff, right? Everyone worries a little bit about money, especially with groceries being so expensive lately—like, I went to the store the other day and a carton of eggs was just ridiculously priced, and I remember standing there thinking about how much everything has gone up. And my family, well, I check in on them, obviously. I'll call my mom on Sundays, usually right after I finish my laundry, just to make sure she's doing okay and her arthritis isn't acting up too badly because the damp weather really gets to her joints. But it's not this constant, overwhelming worry. 

It's not like I'm sitting at home on my couch, staring at the wall, biting my nails, and agonizing over my health or my bank account or anything like that. I pay my bills on time, I try to eat reasonably well—you know, packing a decent lunch for work instead of just hitting the drive-thru every day, maybe a turkey sandwich and some carrots—and I just go about my business. When I'm not at the site, when I don't have that heavy paddle in my hand and the high-vis vest on, I actually feel pretty... well, I wouldn't say relaxed, but I'm definitely not consumed by worry about everyday things. My mind isn't racing with all these "what-ifs" about finances or health. It's really just the blankness at work that terrifies me. Everything else in my life, the day-to-day stuff, it's all pretty manageable. I don't lay awake at night stressing about it, you know? It's just... normal. Just regular life stuff, nothing that takes over my brain like those moments on the job do.

Well, no, not really. I mean, my heart pounds, yes, absolutely, it just hammers in my chest like a jackhammer on the asphalt, but... as for other sudden things? No, I don't think so. I'm not, you know, gasping for air or feeling like I'm choking or dizzy or anything like that. I don't get sweaty palms or feel like the world is spinning out of control or that I'm going to pass out right there on the pavement. 

It's really just... the blankness. And the heart pounding, of course, because when you realize your brain has just completely shut off and you're standing there holding up traffic on a busy county road, it's terrifying. I mean, wouldn't your heart pound? But it's not like a whole body thing, if that makes sense. It's not like I'm having some kind of... I don't know, physical collapse. I'm just standing there, frozen, staring at the forms on my clipboard, the ones with the permit numbers I mentioned, or holding the paddle, and my mind is just an empty void. And my heart is racing because I know I need to do something, I know I need to flip the paddle or radio the other flagger down the line, but the instructions are just gone. 

So, yeah, no other sudden physical things. No shaking, no nausea, no tingling in my fingers. Just the absolute terror of the blankness and my heart beating out of my chest because of it. It's really just isolated to that. I just stand there, looking perfectly normal on the outside, I suppose, in my high-vis gear, while inside my head it's just... nothing. Just a terrifying nothingness.

```json
{"intent": "Screen for seizure aura symptoms such as déjà vu or unusual sensory phenomena", "question": "Right before your mind goes blank, do you ever experience any unusual sensations, such

Like... like a warning sign? No. No, not at all. I don't get any weird tastes in my mouth or, you know, smell burnt toast or whatever it is people say happens. And déjà vu? I mean, honestly, my whole job is kind of repetitive, right? You stand there, you turn the sign from 'STOP' to 'SLOW', you wave the cars through, you wait for the pilot car to come back around... so in a way, everything I do feels like I've done it a million times before, because I have. I've stood on that same stretch of county highway, holding the exact same fiberglass pole, looking at the exact same line of pine trees and the same dented guardrail so many times. But it's not that spooky, weird déjà vu feeling you get where time feels wrong or something mystical is happening. It's just... normal reality. 

Right before the blankness hits, everything is just completely, perfectly normal. I'll be smelling the diesel exhaust from the big rigs passing by, or maybe the hot asphalt if the paving crew is laying down a new layer, or just the damp dirt if it rained the night before. I'll be hearing the static on my two-way radio, maybe my supervisor calling out a lane shift, or the beep-beep-beep of a backhoe reversing. All completely normal sensory stuff. 

And then... snap. It's just gone. The slate is wiped clean. There's no build-up, no strange aura, no fuzzy vision or ringing in my ears to warn me that it's coming. If I had a warning, maybe I could, I don't know, radio somebody to take over for a minute, or step off the shoulder so I'm not in danger. But I don't. It just goes from the noisy, smelly, totally normal construction site straight into that awful, terrifying empty void where I don't even know what the clipboard in my hand is for. So, yeah, no unusual sensations at all. Just the normal world, and then... nothing.
Has anything particularly frightening or traumatic ever happened to you or someone else while you were working on the road?

No, thank God. I mean, it's a dangerous job, you know? You're standing out there with cars whipping by at fifty, sixty miles an hour, and sometimes people are on their phones, or they're just not paying attention, or they're mad that they have to wait. I've had people yell at me, throw things out their windows—one guy tossed a half-empty soda cup that splashed all over my boots, which was just completely unnecessary and ruined my morning, honestly, because then I smelled like stale cola until my lunch break. But as for something truly traumatic? Like an accident, or someone getting hit? No, nothing like that. 

I've been lucky, I suppose. Or maybe just really careful. I always make sure I'm standing exactly where the safety manual says to stand, you know, on the shoulder, giving myself an escape route just in case a driver doesn't see the signs. I've seen some close calls, sure. Like this one time, a couple of months ago, maybe late October because the leaves were just starting to turn that really bright orange, a guy in a silver pickup truck came barreling down the hill and clearly hadn't seen the 'Be Prepared to Stop' sign a mile back. He slammed on his brakes so hard the tires smoked, and he skidded to a stop maybe ten feet from my toes. I could smell the burning rubber for the rest of my shift. My heart was in my throat, obviously, but he didn't hit me, he didn't hit the car in front of him, and nobody got hurt. 

So, no, I haven't been through any big, horrible trauma out there. It's just the everyday stress of the job, the noise, the weather, the angry drivers. Nothing that would... I don't know, nothing that would break my brain and make it just turn off like it does. The job is just the job, you know? It's not a war zone, even if it feels a little chaotic sometimes when the paving machines are running and the dump trucks are backing up with those loud alarms. But nobody's gotten hurt on my watch. Not me, not anyone else.

```json
{"intent": "Assess for motor manifestations of seizures such as eyelid fluttering, staring, or automatisms observed by others", "question": "Has anyone ever told you that your eyes flutter,

Flutter? Like... like rapid blinking or twitching? No, no one has ever mentioned anything like that to me. 

I mean, I work with a crew of about six to eight people usually, depending on the size of the paving job or the lane closure, and we've got the foreman—usually this guy Mike—driving up and down the line in his white Ford F-250 all day long, just checking on us, making sure the cones are straight and traffic is flowing. And then there's the pilot car driver, who literally drives past me and looks right at me every ten or fifteen minutes when they loop back around with a new line of cars. You'd think if I was standing out there on the shoulder fluttering my eyes or twitching or doing something totally bizarre with my face, one of them would have brought it up, right? 

Construction crews aren't exactly shy about pointing out when you look weird or if you're doing something wrong. If I was out there blinking like a broken traffic light, Mike would be on the two-way radio in two seconds asking what the heck is wrong with me. But all they ever say, if they happen to notice the blankness at all, is that I missed a radio call or that I was too slow to flip the paddle. They'll just say something like, "Hey, earth to major Tom," or ask if I fell asleep with my eyes open. 

But nobody has ever said, "Hey, your eyes were fluttering," or that I was making weird movements or anything like that. From what I understand, I just look like I'm standing there. Like a statue, I guess. A statue in a very bright, very unflattering yellow and orange reflective jacket. But no fluttering, no. I'm pretty sure I'd know—or at least someone on the crew would definitely tease me about it or report it—if my face was doing something completely out of my control.

When it ends... it's just awful. I don't just snap back to normal and pick up where I left off, no. I am so incredibly confused. In fact, that's really the main reason I came in to see someone, because my mind keeps going blank at the absolute worst times. 

I'll come out of that void, and I'll just be standing there on the shoulder of the highway, and I will look at the road-closure forms on my clipboard—the exact same forms I have to fill out every single shift, logging the cone placements and the lane tapers—or I'll look at the stop-slow paddle in my hand, and I suddenly cannot remember the steps I have done for years. It's like I've never seen them before. I'll stare at the big red octagon on the paddle, and my brain is just... empty. 

I know I'm supposed to be doing something, you know? I can see the line of cars waiting, I can hear the diesel engines idling, and the pilot car is probably heading back my way, but I just stand there staring at the paddle trying to remember how my job works. I've been doing this for years, day in and day out, in the rain and the heat, and suddenly the basic steps of turning the sign or radioing the other flagger are just gone from my head. It's like all the files in my brain were dumped out onto the floor. It takes me a while to piece reality back together, to remember what the forms are for and what the paddle means. It's terrifying, honestly, because I have two-ton vehicles right next to me and my mind is just wiped completely blank. I just feel so lost until it finally clicks back into place.

```json

Yeah... yes, I have. Very much so. It's not just a passing bad mood, either. It's... well, most mornings, honestly, I wake up and there is just this—this heavy, hollow sadness sitting right in the middle of my chest. It's like a physical weight, you know? I'll open my eyes, and before I even look at the alarm clock, before I even throw the covers off or put my feet on the floor, I just feel like the entire day is already ruined. 

Like, what is even the point of getting up? I'll just lie there and stare at the ceiling—it's got those little popcorn bumps, the kind they used to put in apartments years ago—and I'll just trace the patterns and feel this absolute, crushing dread. It takes everything I have just to force myself to sit up. And it's been like this for weeks now. 

I used to at least enjoy my morning coffee, just sitting by the window in my kitchen for ten minutes before I had to go put on all that heavy high-vis gear and stand out in the exhaust fumes all day. But lately, I don't even care about that. The coffee just tastes like hot, dirty water, and that heavy feeling in my chest just doesn't lift. It follows me to the bathroom while I'm brushing my teeth, it follows me out to my car... I'll be driving out to the job site, gripping the steering wheel, and I just feel so incredibly down, like I'm completely hollowed out inside. I don't know how else to explain it, but it's just this constant, suffocating sadness that makes everything feel completely pointless before the sun even comes up.
How has your sleep been over the past few weeks?

My sleep? Oh, it's... it's been terrible. Just absolutely terrible. I mean, I used to be the kind of person who could sleep through anything, you know? Back when I first started flagging, I'd come home so exhausted from standing on the asphalt all day that I'd just crash. But over the last few weeks, it's like my body has just forgotten how to rest. 

I'll go to bed, right? I'll do my whole routine—brush my teeth, wash my face, make sure my uniform is laid out for the next morning so I don't have to think about it when I wake up—and I'll get into bed. The sheets are clean, the room is dark, everything is exactly how it should be. But I just lie there. I'll stare at the glowing red numbers on the alarm clock—11:00, 11:30, 12:15—and my mind just won't shut off. Or, well, it's not even that my mind is racing with thoughts, it's just that heavy, awful feeling keeping me awake. 

And then, if I do finally manage to drift off, it's not real sleep. It's that shallow, restless kind where you feel like you're still half awake. I'll toss and turn, and the blankets will get all tangled up around my legs. And then I'll wake up at, like, 3:00 in the morning. Wide awake. Just staring at the ceiling again, tracing those popcorn bumps in the dark, feeling that dread settling into my chest. I'll try to go back to sleep, I really will. I'll try counting backwards from a hundred, or taking deep breaths, all those things people tell you to do. But it never works. I just lie there for hours until the alarm finally goes off at 5:00 AM, and I have to drag myself out of bed feeling completely drained, like I haven't slept in a month. It makes the days out on the road so much harder to get through, feeling this exhausted on top of everything else.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite recently?

My appetite? Oh... yeah. Yeah, there's been a big change there, too. It's like... food just doesn't mean anything to me anymore. I used to pack these really good lunches for work, you know? Because when you're out on the road, standing on the asphalt for eight, ten hours a day, you need fuel. I'd make these big turkey sandwiches with the thick-cut bacon and the good cheddar cheese, and I'd bring a thermos of hot soup in the winter, or a big container of cold pasta salad in the summer. I used to actually look forward to my lunch break. I'd sit on the tailgate of my truck, or in the cab if it was raining, and just enjoy eating. 

But lately? Lately, I don't even bother packing anything. I just... I don't care. The thought of eating just feels like a chore, like chewing cardboard. I'll go the whole shift, standing out there with the stop-slow paddle, breathing in the dust and the exhaust, and I won't even realize I haven't eaten until the end of the day. I just skip meals completely without even noticing. It's not like I'm trying to diet or anything, the hunger just isn't there. The hollow feeling in my chest just sort of takes up all the space where my appetite used to be.

And it's really starting to show, honestly. I put on my high-vis pants the other day—the ones with the reflective stripes around the calves that I've worn for the last three years—and I had to cinch my belt up two extra notches just to keep them from sliding down my hips. They're so loose on me now, they just kind of bag around my legs. And my sister came over on Sunday to drop off some mail that got delivered to her house by mistake, and the first thing she said when I opened the door was, "My god, why do you look so drawn?" She kept asking if I was sick, if I was eating enough, because apparently my face has gotten all hollowed out. I looked in the mirror after she left, really looked, and she was right. I just look so... depleted. But even knowing that, even seeing how much weight I've lost, I still can't bring myself to care enough to make a sandwich.
With everything feeling so heavy and difficult, have you had any thoughts of wanting to end your life or that you would be better off dead?

Yeah... it’s hard to talk about, but... yes. I have. It’s like what I was saying about feeling so completely depleted. I used to try to push those kinds of dark thoughts away, you know? When you're out there on a two-lane highway with logging trucks flying past you at sixty miles an hour, you have to stay sharp, you have to actually care about staying safe. 

But now... I just do not have the energy to fight the thought anymore. It just sits there in my head, especially when I'm lying awake in the middle of the night staring at that ceiling, and I just keep thinking that it might be better if I just did not wake up. Just... didn't open my eyes. Didn't have to face the alarm clock or the exhaust fumes or that terrible, crushing weight in my chest. I don't even picture doing anything violent, it's just this overwhelming desire to just stop. To finally get to rest and never have to drag myself out of bed again. 

And the thing is, it’s not just staying inside my head anymore. It really scares my family because I have started saying it out loud. Like when my sister was here on Sunday, after she told me how hollowed out I looked, I just kind of stared at the floor and said, "I really wish I just wouldn't wake up tomorrow." I didn't even mean to say it, it just slipped out because it's always right there at the front of my mind now. And the look on her face... she looked so horrified, so terrified for me. She started crying and asking what I meant. But I couldn't even take it back or try to comfort her, because it's the truth. I'm just too tired to pretend I want to be here anymore.

Worthlessness... yeah. That's... that's basically all I feel anymore. It's like my brain has just become this projector that won't turn off, and it just keeps replaying every single little thing I've failed to do for the people in my life. Just over and over, playing on a loop, especially when I'm lying awake in the middle of the night.

And the community choir I used to be in—I sang alto, and we had this whole seasonal program planned out, and I just stopped going to rehearsals. I left the director completely scrambling to cover my parts at the last minute, and I didn't even have the decency to send an email explaining why. 

And my own family... I mean, you heard how I treated my sister on Sunday. She comes out of her way to bring me my mail, she's clearly worried sick about me, and I can't even offer her a glass of water. I just dump all that heaviness on her and make her cry. I don't help my parents out with their yard work anymore, I don't call anyone back. I just lie there in bed, replaying all these failures, every little thing I didn't do, and I just feel like I am a completely useless person. Utterly useless. I've let down my friend, the choir, my family... everyone who relies on me. And honestly, when I think about how terrible I've been to all of them, I really feel like I deserve whatever punishment is coming to me. I just deserve it. I'm just taking up space at this point.

Able to keep up? No... no, I'm really not keeping up at all. I've completely stopped functioning, honestly. Like with my job... I just stopped being reliable at work entirely. People think being a flagger is just standing there holding a sign, but there's so much more to it, and I just couldn't do it anymore. It started with the road-closure paperwork. Whenever we set up a work zone, there are these detailed logs and closure forms you have to fill out—recording the exact times the advance warning signs go up, the mile markers, the taper lengths for the cones. I used to do it in my sleep, but lately, I would just stare at the clipboard, and the words wouldn't make any sense. I just could not finish the road-closure paperwork. My brain felt like it was full of wet sand.

And then it got to the point where I couldn't even trust myself with the actual traffic-safety steps. That's the really terrifying part, because you have the road crew's lives in your hands, not to mention the drivers. You have to be constantly communicating on the two-way radio, making sure the pilot car is clear, flipping the stop-slow paddle at the exact right second... and I just couldn't focus. I'd be out there, completely numb, and realize I hadn't checked the radio clearance before thinking about letting a line of cars through. I couldn't trust myself to keep people safe anymore, so I just stopped being able to do the job. 

And it bled into everything else, too. I completely pulled away from everything that used to matter to me. I told you about abandoning the choir, but I also stopped showing up for my volunteering shifts. I used to go down to the county animal shelter every Saturday morning to help walk the bigger dogs that pull too hard for the older volunteers, and I just stopped going. Didn't call, didn't explain. I just pulled away from the choir, the volunteering, and my family... completely isolated myself. I wouldn't answer the phone, wouldn't leave my house. It got to the point where my family was so terrified by how completely I'd shut down and stopped functioning that they finally intervened. They're the ones who felt they had to bring me for help today. Because left to my own devices, I wouldn't have even made it out the front door. I just can't manage any of it anymore.
Have you ever had periods in your life where you felt unusually energized, euphoric, or on top of the world, needing very little sleep?

No... no, I can't say that I have. I mean, I've had good days, sure, back before all this... this crushing weight started, but never anything like what you're describing. I've never felt euphoric or like I was buzzing with energy or anything like that. 

And I have certainly never been the kind of person who doesn't need sleep. Honestly, I've always been someone who really, really relies on getting a full night's rest. When you work out on the roads like I do—or did, I guess—standing on the asphalt for eight or ten hours a day, dealing with the elements, the sun beating down on you or the wind just cutting right through your high-vis jacket... you absolutely have to sleep. I would always make sure I was in bed by a reasonable hour, because if I didn't get my solid seven or eight hours, I would be completely dragging the next day. I was never one of those people who could just run on fumes. 

Even way back when I was getting my bachelor's degree, I would see these other students pulling all-nighters, drinking all those energy drinks and acting like they were completely on top of the world the next morning, and I just never understood it. My brain just doesn't work that way. I've always needed my rest to function. So, no, I've never had a period where I felt like I didn't need sleep or had all this endless, unnatural energy. My life has usually just been a steady, predictable baseline of normal energy. Well, until recently, of course, where it's just... nothing. Just complete, heavy exhaustion. But I've never experienced the opposite of that, no.
Have you ever gone through a period like this before in your life where you felt this depressed and down?

Before this? I... I don't even know if 'before' really exists anymore, to be perfectly honest with you. Because this... this current stretch has just been going on for so, so long. It hasn't just been a few bad weeks or a rough patch. This heavy depression, this constant, suffocating guilt about every little thing, the completely drained, low energy, and just... the total loss of appetite... all of that has been with me for about a year and two months now. 

Fourteen whole months. I remember when it first really started to settle in, it was like this massive, dark curtain just dropped over my life and it hasn't lifted for a single second since. At first, I tried to convince myself I was just burned out, you know? Just tired from standing on the asphalt all day, dealing with the traffic and the weather. But then the weeks turned into months, and I just kept sinking deeper and deeper. The guilt just wrapped around my throat, and my energy completely vanished to the point where just pulling the blankets off myself in the morning felt like I was trying to move a mountain. 

And food... I mean, for the last year and two months, I haven't even wanted to look at a plate of food. I used to actually like making dinner, trying new recipes and things, but now just the thought of chewing feels like too much work, too much effort that I just don't have. So, when you ask if I've had periods like this before... I just keep thinking about how this one period has completely swallowed up the last year and two months of my life. It's just been one long, endless nightmare, day in and day out, without a single break.
